name: Estimate distances by eye
blurb: Useful for hiking, driving, photography and shooting. It is calibration, not talent: you learn what known distances look like and then interpolate.
gear: A measured 100 m course, or a map
A rangefinder or a phone map for checking
steps: Calibrate on known distances: pace out 50, 100 and 200 metres and study how a person, a car and a tree look at each.
Learn the detail markers: at 100 m you can see faces; at 200 m faces blur; at 400 m a person is a shape with distinguishable limbs; beyond 800 m a person is a dot.
Learn the bracketing method: estimate the maximum and minimum plausible distances and take the middle.
Learn the unit-of-measure method: judge how many 100 m sections fit between you and the object.
Learn the distortions: distances over water, snow or into the sun read short; uphill and in poor light read long.
Practise daily with a guess-then-check loop using a map or rangefinder.
tips: Objects seen across a valley are almost always further than they look.
Regular calibration matters. This skill decays quickly without the feedback loop.
proof: Ten estimates between 50 m and 1 km, each within 20% of the real distance.
